code:
SELECT p.FirstName, p.LastName, e.JobTitle, e.HireDate
FROM Person.Person AS p
JOIN HumanResources.Employee AS e
  ON e.BusinessEntityID = p.BusinessEntityID;
caption: Every Employee IS a Person — but not every Person is an Employee (customers, vendors too).

eyebrow: The trick: PK = FK on the same column
code:
-- Employee.BusinessEntityID is BOTH:
--   its own PRIMARY KEY, and
--   a FOREIGN KEY to Person.BusinessEntityID

CREATE TABLE dbo.Employee (
  PersonID INT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY
    REFERENCES dbo.Person (PersonID),
  JobTitle NVARCHAR(50)
);
caption: A primary key can't repeat — so at most ONE Employee row can exist per PersonID.

eyebrow: When to split into two tables at all
code:
-- Split into two 1:1 tables when...
-- one side is optional (not every Person is an Employee)
-- one side has rarely-used columns
-- you're modeling supertype/subtype
caption: If two things always pair up exactly, you'd usually just use one table instead.
